1:
The second round of the debate opens with Eliphaz the Temanite, and the witnesses set the scene before a single word of his speech is weighed. The reformed John Gill marks the man and the moment: Eliphaz was the first of Job's three friends and comforters, the oldest of them and the one who had opened the dispute at the beginning; the argument had since been carried on by Bildad and Zophar in their turns, and now, the course coming round again, it fell to him to answer a second time, as here he does. The Targum styles him one "who was of Teman," and he is the senior speaker, so that the weight of his years lends a borrowed authority to the reproof he is about to level.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the opening the temper of a man stung. Eliphaz falls very foul upon Job, Henry says, because Job had contradicted what he and his colleagues had said and would not acquiesce in it and applaud it as they expected; and proud people are apt to take it much amiss if they may not dictate and give law to all about them, censuring as ignorant and obstinate all who cannot in everything say as they say. Several grave crimes Eliphaz will charge upon Job in the course of the chapter, Henry notes, and for no better reason than that Job would not own himself a hypocrite. It is common, he adds, for angry disputants to represent one another's reasonings as impertinent and ridiculous, more than there is cause, forgetting the doom pronounced upon him that calls his brother Raca and Thou fool in Matt. 5:22.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the plan of the whole speech in advance, dividing it into its three movements: Eliphaz charges Job with impiety in attempting to justify himself down to v.13; then asserts the utter corruption and abominable state of man through vv.14-16; and finally, drawing on his own knowledge and the observations of the ancients, paints the desolation to which the wicked are exposed, insinuating all the while that Job has such calamities to dread, from v.17 to the end. The witnesses do not divide over the drift. They agree that the speech is an old man's second attempt to break a sufferer he cannot understand, and that its courtesy is thinner and its accusations sharper than in the first; the comforter of the first cycle has hardened, under contradiction, into a prosecutor.
2:
Eliphaz begins his assault by turning Job's reputation for wisdom against him, asking whether a wise man should "utter vain knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind." The reformed John Gill allows that Job was thought a wise man, or thought himself one, and was so in the best sense, having the fear of God which is the beginning of wisdom; and it ill becomes such a man to utter what the Targum calls windy knowledge, empty and unsolid, that swells and puffs up and is knowledge falsely so called. Yet Gill quietly enters his demurrer: it does not appear that Job had in fact uttered such vain and fruitless things as deserved to be compared to the wind.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch open the strophe by reading the interrogative He as in ch. 13:25, and weigh the two nouns. Wind is the opposite of what is solid and sure, and the "east wind" in the parallel, as in Hosea 12:2, signifies what is worthless with the added notion of vehement, blustering action; the "belly" they refuse to set as the mere opposite of the heart. Eliphaz, on their reading, takes Job's detailed and bitter answers for empty words and impassioned tirades that ill become a man who claims to be wise, as Job had claimed at ch. 12:3 and ch. 13:2.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke would render the first line, "Should a wise man utter the science of wind?" a science without solidity or certainty; and he fixes the physiology, taking the word for "belly" of the cavity of the body, here the lungs and cheeks and throat that fill with breath. The east wind, he notes, is the stormy kadim of the Levant, the same tempestuous blast named at Acts 27:14, so that Eliphaz means Job's speech to have been a very storm and hurricane of words. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, draws the plain inference the taunt intends: Job therefore is not wise, and his words have been vain and windy. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "fill" as satisfy the mind and conscience, and "east wind" as discourses not merely unprofitable but pernicious, hurtful to the speaker and his hearers alike.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the charge of windy knowledge the accusation of downright folly and absurdity: whereas Job had been reputed a wise man, Eliphaz would have it that he had now forfeited the reputation, talking so extravagantly and so little to the purpose that any one would say his wisdom had departed from him — the very note Bildad had struck at ch. 8:2 and Zophar at ch. 11:2. There is indeed in the world, Henry grants, a great deal of vain knowledge, a science falsely so called that puffs a man up with a fond conceit of his own attainments and is worthless for all that; and unprofitable talk is evil talk, for we must give account in the great day not only for wicked words but for idle words, and speeches that do no service to God or our neighbour were better left unspoken. So the witnesses converge on the sting, even as Gill quietly demurs from its justice.
3:
The taunt of windy speech is pressed into a sharper form, as Eliphaz asks whether a wise man should "reason with unprofitable talk." The reformed John Gill takes the question as a challenge to the very manner of Job's discourse: does it become a wise man to talk such idle stuff, things false and foolish and frothy, that minister no grace to the hearer and serve no use of edifying? Nothing is profitable, Gill urges, but what tends to increase solid wisdom and spiritual knowledge, to exercise grace and shape a holy life; and the fit matter for a wise and good man's mouth is the doctrines of the word of God and the experiences of his grace, communicated by his people one to another. He who deals in words of no profit can hardly expect to convince men of their errors or reprove their sins with any success.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the charge a more pointed theological edge. To "reason with unprofitable talk," he suggests, is to talk disrespectfully of one's Maker, to speak to him or of him without reverence, and then to suppose one has proved something when one has only uttered words of little meaning, and used sound in the place of sense. On Clarke's reading the accusation is not merely that Job's arguments are thin but that they border on irreverence, a heedless handling of holy things.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott concentrates the whole verse into a single dismissive verdict: Job's arguments, though pretentious and apparently recondite, are for all that unprofitable, and can do no good. So the three witnesses stand together over the drift of the taunt, that Job's speeches are so much noise without substance. Yet it is worth marking, as the earlier verse showed, that this is Eliphaz's estimate and not the narrator's; the reader who has heard Job wrestle honestly with the hiding of God's face may judge that the "unprofitable talk" of a suffering man contained more truth than the polished maxims his friends prefer, and that the charge of empty speech comes with an ill grace from those whose comfort has so far comforted nothing. The movement of the argument here is all downward pressure, an attempt to shame Job into silence before the substance of his case is so much as touched, and it prepares the graver accusations of impiety that the next verses will bring. Gill's own rule stands quietly against the accuser: the only speech that truly profits is that which ministers grace to the hearer and tends to edifying, and by that measure it is not at all clear whose words in this long debate have been the more unprofitable — the sufferer's honest complaint, or the comforters' polished maxims that have healed nothing.
4:
"Yea, thou castest off fear, and restrainest prayer before God" — with these words the taunt of folly hardens into a charge of impiety, and the witnesses gather to test both its terms and its justice. The reformed John Gill insists that the "fear" here cast off cannot be the grace of fear that Job truly possessed, for that is a blessing of the covenant, one of the gifts that are without repentance, a part of internal grace that can never be finally lost; it may rather mean the whole worship of God, the outward form of religion, which is sometimes signified by the fear of the Lord. What Job could never do was throw away the reverence that was rooted in him by grace.

The wesleyan-arminian voices read the accusation more starkly. Adam Clarke hears Eliphaz saying that Job has no reverence for God, and that instead of humbling himself and making supplication to his Judge he spends his time arraigning providence and justifying himself; and Clarke turns it into counsel, that a troubled soul does better to run at once to God for pardon than to linger over excuses for its conduct. John Wesley glosses "thou makest void fear" as an assault on piety and religion itself, wrought by Job's unworthy speeches and by the pernicious principle that God makes no difference between good and bad in the course of his providence; and to "restrain prayer" is, as far as in Job lies, to banish prayer out of the world by making it seem useless. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical witness, adds that Job's tendency to a kind of fatalism, as in ch. 12:16-25, would naturally check the offering of prayer and set an example likely to lead to murmuring and blasphemy.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees the whole of religion summed up in the two things named, fearing God and praying to him, the former the most needful principle and the latter the most needful practice; those who restrain prayer give evidence that they have cast off fear, for the prayerless are fearless and graceless. Yet Henry is scrupulously fair: this charge upon Job, he says, was utterly false, though it wanted not some colour; and much of it Eliphaz merely inferred from Job's doctrine, reasoning that if a good man may be so afflicted, then farewell prayer and the fear of God, as the tempted heart complains in Mal. 3:14 and Ps. 73:13. It is a piece of injustice, Henry warns, of which even wise and good men are guilty in the heat of dispute, to charge upon their adversaries the consequences of opinions which those adversaries abhor.
5:
Eliphaz now claims to catch Job's guilt in the very act of speaking, for "thy mouth uttereth thine iniquity, and thou choosest the tongue of the crafty." The reformed John Gill takes the mouth as betraying the heart: the wickedness within prompted the words without, so that Job's speech proved him and was an evidence against him; and had the fear of God been before his eyes he would have bridled his lips, since the man who bridles not his tongue has a religion that is vain, as James 1:26 declares. The "tongue of the crafty" Gill reads as the varnish that covers the fault.

Here a real difference of construction surfaces. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets out the two readings plainly: either "thy mouth teacheth thine iniquity," so that the mouth proclaims a sin the crafty tongue tries to conceal, or "thine iniquity teacheth thy mouth," so that the wickedness within schools the lips in their eloquence and by consequence chooses the language of the cunning. Ellicott inclines to the latter, though he grants that the next verse rather favours the former, and Gill too records both turns of the clause. The disagreement is genuine, if quiet: does the mouth betray the iniquity, or does the iniquity tutor the mouth?

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leaves no doubt of the malice he hears in "the tongue of the crafty." Job, he says, has used sophistical arguments and varnished his own conduct, resembling those cunning persons whose subtlety is derived from the old serpent, the nachash who was more subtle than any beast of the field in Gen. 3:1; such wisdom is not from above but from beneath. John Wesley agrees that Job speaks wickedly and craftily, covering impious principles with fair pretences of piety. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sharpens the accusation to its worst point: to utter iniquity is bad, but to teach it is worse, for the mouth of iniquity could do little mischief without the tongue of the crafty, mixing some good words with the bad as tradesmen mix their wares to help them off; and it is bad to break the least commandment, but worse to teach men so, as Matt. 5:19 warns. The witnesses agree on the charge Eliphaz levels; they differ only on which way the Hebrew clause is to be turned, and Henry adds that honesty, in the end, is the best policy. Beneath the shared accusation, then, lies a small but genuine crux of syntax, on which the schools quietly part even while they stand together in reading Eliphaz to mean that Job has clothed a wicked heart in a crafty and plausible tongue — a charge that says more, perhaps, of the accuser's suspicion than of the words it professes to interpret.
6:
Eliphaz seals his indictment with a flourish of the courtroom: "thine own mouth condemneth thee, and not I; yea, thine own lips testify against thee." The reformed John Gill unfolds the legal figure with relish. Job is convicted out of his own mouth, so that Eliphaz is spared the trouble of passing sentence; the accused man's own lips are at once judge and jury and witness, bringing in the verdict and pronouncing it, and standing, as the proverb has it, instead of a thousand witnesses. There is a certain triumph in the disclaimer "and not I," as though Eliphaz would keep his own hands clean and let Job be his own executioner.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry grants the principle but denies the fairness. It is true, he says, that those are most effectually condemned who are condemned by themselves, as Titus 3:11 and Luke 19:22 both show, and many a man needs no more to sink him than to have his own tongue fall upon him. But Eliphaz should have considered that he and his fellows had provoked Job to say the very things they now take advantage of; and to draw a man into hasty words and then arraign him for them is not fair dealing. The self-condemnation is real, Henry allows, but the manner of exacting it is unjust.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch look ahead from the verdict to the taunt it introduces, for with the challenge of the next line — art thou the first man that was born? — Eliphaz assumes that the first created man, coming straight from the hand of God at the world's beginning, would have had the most direct and profound insight into its mysteries. They recall the ironical Hindu proverb Schlottmann cites, "Yea, indeed, he is the first man; no wonder that he is so wise," and they are careful that the Hebrew is not to be rendered "wast thou born as the first man," but keeps its edge as pure sarcasm. The witnesses do not divide over the meaning of the verse; they divide only in temper, Gill savouring the neatness of the self-conviction, Henry protesting the injustice of a charge wrung from provoked speech, and Keil and Delitzsch turning to prepare the reader for the mockery of Job's pretended antiquity that immediately follows. It is a shrewd rhetorical stroke, this handing of the sword to the accused; but it is also, as Henry sees, a way of evading responsibility, for Eliphaz would have the guilt of the sentence rest wholly on Job's lips and none of it on his own, when in truth the friends had baited the very words they now hold up as proof.
7:
"Art thou the first man that was born? or wast thou made before the hills?" The mockery of Job's supposed wisdom now takes a grand and ancient form, and the witnesses trace its several barbs. The reformed John Gill hears Eliphaz asking whether Job imagines himself to be the first Adam, created in wisdom and knowledge, who knew so much of God and of nature that he gave the creatures their names, until by grasping unlawfully after more he lost much of what he had; or whether Job fancies he has lived ever since that beginning and gathered, by long experience through all the ages, a fund of knowledge beyond other men.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke renders the first line "Wert thou born before Adam?" and reads the whole as a rebuke to Job's presumption: art thou in the pristine state of purity and innocence, or like Adam in his first estate? It does not become the fallen descendant of a fallen parent to talk as Job does. And the second line — made before the hills — he takes as asking whether God created Job at the beginning of his ways, the first intelligent creature his hands had formed. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, fixes the polemical point precisely: the taunt is a retort upon ch. 12:2 and following, where Job had claimed that even the inanimate creation could teach his friends what they professed to know, so that Eliphaz flings his own words back at him.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the assumption that gives the sarcasm its force, that the first-created man, born directly of God before the world was fully formed, would have the deepest insight into its secrets. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the sneer into its full shape. Job had made only the modest demand of ch. 12:3, "allow that I have understanding as well as you"; but because he would not grant them the monopoly of wisdom, they will have it that he claims it all to himself, as though he were senior to all mankind, prior even to Adam, or made before the hills as Wisdom herself was in Prov. 8:23. Must God's counsels, Henry has Eliphaz demand, which are as the great mountains of Ps. 36:6 and immovable as the everlasting hills, be subject to Job's notions and bow to them? The witnesses agree that the question is pure irony, meant to shrink Job's claim to parity of knowledge into a monstrous pretension he never made.
8:
The mockery climbs from the first man to the very council-chamber of heaven, as Eliphaz asks, "Hast thou heard the secret of God? and dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself?" The reformed John Gill reads it as an inquiry whether Job has stood in the privy council of God, been one of his cabinet counsellors, and been let into all the secrets of his purposes and providence and the reasons of his administrations, that he talks so freely and so boldly. Only the Son of God, Gill observes, was truly the Angel of the great council, in the Father's bosom and privy to all his thoughts; yet he grants that there are secrets which God makes known to them that fear him, the secrets of his love and of the covenant of grace, and that Job in some measure was acquainted with these.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the questions as strong sarcasm uttered with great contempt. "Hast thou hearkened in God's council?" he paraphrases: wert thou one of the celestial cabinet when God said, Let us make man in our image? And to "restrain wisdom to thyself" is to behave as if God's counsels had been revealed to none but Job, so that all the world must take on trust whatever he is pleased to speak.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch look forward to the "consolations of God" that this strophe will name, understanding by them the promises, framed to God's majesty and will, by which the friends had sought to cheer Job, presupposing a humble resignation to the just hand of God; and they gloss the "word spoken gently" as the mild tone the friends claim to have kept, the soft-flowing laat that recalls the gently murmuring waters of Siloah in Isa. 8:6. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the same disdain: does Job pretend to be of the cabinet-council of heaven, that he can give better reasons than others for God's proceedings? There are secret things of God, Henry cautions, which belong not to us and which we must not presume to account for, and those are daringly presumptuous who try. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Eliphaz is charging Job with an arrogance he never claimed, turning Job's honest confession of ignorance into a pretended intimacy with the mind of God. There is an irony the reader may feel that the witnesses only touch: Eliphaz mocks Job for pretending to overhear the counsels of God, while himself speaking with an unshaken confidence about why God afflicts men — as though the secret of God were open to the accuser and closed only to the accused.
9:
The sarcasm sharpens into a direct comparison of wits: "What knowest thou, that we know not? what understandest thou, which is not in us?" The reformed John Gill notes at once that these are very nearly Job's own words thrown back at him, for Job had said as much to his friends at ch. 13:2, "what ye know, the same do I know also." What Job had urged as a plea for parity, Eliphaz now flings back as a taunt of presumption, matching claim against claim.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills out the challenge into a demand for proof. Is it likely, Eliphaz asks, that Job's intellect is greater than theirs, or that he has cultivated his understanding better than they have cultivated ours? Let him show them, then, any single point of knowledge that he possesses and they do not, any truth that lies in him and is not equally in them. The challenge is meant to be unanswerable, or rather to be answered only by an embarrassed silence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the exchange with a rueful eye for the psychology of controversy. Job had claimed only an equal standing in knowledge, but eager disputants, Henry observes, think they have a privilege to commend themselves and to disparage their opponents; and so they return upon him, "What knowest thou that we know not?" How natural such replies are in the heat of argument, he remarks, and how simple they look afterwards, upon the review. There is a quiet lesson in the way both sides have now used the very same words: Job to say he is no fool, his friends to say he is no oracle. The witnesses, few as they are here, agree that the verse is a specimen of the pride that creeps into good men's disputes, each party grasping at the reputation of wisdom and grudging it to the other. What began as a search for truth has become a contest for the last word; and the tragedy, as the whole chapter shows, is that neither the knowledge Job claims nor the knowledge his friends boast has yet touched the real wound, which is not a want of information about God but the felt absence of God himself. The taunt is clever, but it is idle, for it moves the debate not one step nearer to the thing that Job most needs to have answered. The parity of knowledge that Job had pleaded as the ground for carrying his cause past his friends to God, Eliphaz can only hear as a bid for supremacy among men; and so the two sides talk past each other, the one asking to be heard and the other refusing to grant that anything worth hearing could come from a mouth it has already condemned.
10:
Against Job's claim to knowledge Eliphaz sets the authority of age: "With us are both the grayheaded and very aged men, much elder than thy father." The reformed John Gill notes that the word is singular, the gray-headed man, and that gray hairs are at once a sign of old age and an emblem of wisdom; Eliphaz seems to answer Job's own hint that wisdom lay with him because he was ancient, by claiming the greater antiquity for his own side. It is the appeal, familiar in every age, to the settled weight of the elders against the upstart.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke cites a Chaldee paraphrase that names the men outright — "Truly Eliphaz the hoary-headed, and Bildad the long-lived, are among us; and Zophar, who in age surpasseth thy father" — and judges that Eliphaz refers to himself and his two companions rather than to the old men of their tribes or the masters who had taught them. Eliphaz, being seemingly the eldest of the three, takes the lead throughout the poem, and here he plays the card of seniority as his trump.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the appeal and finds it a broken reed. To shelter under the gray heads and the fathers — "we have the fathers on our side; all the ancient doctors are of our opinion" — is a thing soon said but not so soon proved, and, when proved, truth is not so readily discovered by it as most people imagine. Henry sets against it the psalmist's confession in Ps. 119:100, "I understand more than the ancients, because I keep thy precepts," and the later verdict of Elihu at ch. 32:9 that great men are not always wise, neither do the aged always understand judgment. Perhaps, Henry grants, the three friends really were older than Job and thought him bound to defer to them for that alone; but age is no guarantee of wisdom, and the oldest are not always the wisest. And Clarke observes that it is because Eliphaz seems the eldest of the three that he opens each part of this dramatic poem and speaks first, so that the boast of gray hairs is not merely an argument but a claim to the leadership of the debate. The witnesses agree that Eliphaz here leans on the prestige of years where he cannot lean on the strength of argument, and that the appeal, however venerable, decides nothing; a hoary head lends a maxim dignity, but not truth, and the whole later intervention of the young Elihu will be built on the premise that wisdom is the gift of God's breath and not the mere accumulation of days.
11:
Having pressed his age and authority, Eliphaz turns wounded: "Are the consolations of God small with thee? is there any secret thing with thee?" The reformed John Gill takes the "consolations of God" first of the comforts Eliphaz and his friends had offered — the promises that on repentance Job's latter end would exceed his beginning — which they call the consolations of God because administered, as they thought, in his name and according to his will; and he charges Job with having slighted them. But Gill will not stop there, for divine consolations are truly great things, and it is a real charge that Job made light of the comforts of God, Father, Son, and Spirit, each of whom is a comforter.

The wesleyan-arminian voices divide their attention. John Wesley reads the question as Eliphaz's complaint that the comforts propounded on condition of repentance are small and contemptible in Job's eyes, and takes "is there any secret thing with thee?" as asking whether Job has some peculiar, private way of comfort unknown to other men. Adam Clarke, by contrast, spreads before the reader a whole array of ancient renderings, so various that scarcely two translators agree: the Vulgate, "Can it be a hard thing for God to comfort thee, but thou hinderest it by thy intemperate speeches?"; the Syriac and Arabic, "Remove from thee the threatenings of God, and speak tranquilly with thy own spirit"; the Septuagint, that Job has been scourged lightly for his sins yet has spoken beyond all measure; and the plain sense of the Authorized Version, which asks whether some secret sin harboured in the bosom has hindered the operation of divine comfort. Clarke lays them all out and, with unusual reserve, bids the reader choose for himself.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott owns the phrase to be one of the obscure sayings of the book, granting that the Authorized Version yields very good sense while noting that "small with thee" means, of course, too small for thee. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers up the reproach: Eliphaz takes it ill that Job did not value more highly the comforts he and his friends administered, forgetting that though they had said some good things, in their application to Job they were miserable comforters. The consolations of God are not in themselves small, Henry insists — divine comforts are great things — and it is a lamentable thing, and an affront to God, if they be small with us; yet the fault here lay less in Job's contempt of them than in the friends' misapplication. The witnesses agree that Eliphaz mistook the coldness of Job's reception of poor comfort for a contempt of the comfort of God.
12:
Eliphaz reads Job's very looks as symptoms of a mind unhinged: "Why doth thine heart carry thee away? and what do thy eyes wink at?" The reformed John Gill takes the heart's carrying-away as the pull of self-conceit and contempt of others, even to the slighting of God's consolations; the heart, being deceitful and wicked, sometimes carries good men to say and do what ill becomes them, for a man is tempted when he is drawn away of his own lust and enticed, as James 1:14 teaches. If Job was so carried at all, Gill implies, it was his own heart and no other that bore him beyond due bounds.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pictures the scene almost physically. Why does Job conceive such high sentiments of himself, and at what do his eyes wink or flash? Clarke sees an allusion either to the sparkling of the eye in joy or to the furious rolling of the eyes in a man distracted, and quotes Rosenmüller's rendering, "Whither does thy soul hurry thee? what mean thy rolling eyes?" Job seems transported beyond himself, actuated by a furious spirit, beside himself; his words and his very eyes betray it. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical witness, fastens on the winking with a lighter touch: why do the eyes wink, he asks, as though it were only Job who perceived the thing, and all the world besides were blind. John Wesley, another wesleyan-arminian voice, reads the winking as an angry, supercilious, disdainful look, the outward sign of a heart transported by pride into unworthy speech.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the verse in the frame of the whole charge, that Job has set himself in opposition to God. Every man, Henry says, is tempted when he is drawn away of his own lust; if we fly off from God and our duty, or fly out into anything amiss, it is our own heart that carries us away. Why so careless and mindless, Eliphaz seems to ask, hearing what is said as if half asleep, and why so scornful, disdaining our words as if it were below thee to notice them? Henry hears in it an unkind construction put upon a suffering man's distraction. The witnesses do not divide over the sense; they agree that Eliphaz turns the visible marks of Job's anguish — the labouring heart, the restless eye — into evidence of a proud and ungoverned spirit, and reads passion where a more charitable eye would have read pain.
13:
The winking eye and the carried-away heart are traced to their worst issue: "that thou turnest thy spirit against God, and lettest such words go out of thy mouth." The reformed John Gill marks the terrible advance in the accusation. It is not against men, nor against his friends only, that Job is now said to turn, but against God himself, as one filled with wrath and indignation, showing the enmity of his heart, committing acts of hostility, stretching out his hand and strengthening himself against the Almighty — the very image, Gill notes, that the following verses will draw out, of a man running upon God on the thick bosses of his buckler. The charge has grown from folly, through impiety, to open war with heaven.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the gravity of it and the injustice of it together. It was bad, he says, that Job's heart should be carried away from God, but much worse that it should be turned against God; for those who forsake God will soon break out into open enmity to him, setting their mouth against the heavens as the wicked do in Ps. 73:9. Yet Henry protests the want of candour and charity in the reproach. Eliphaz has put the harshest possible construction upon the speeches of a man of settled reputation for piety, now labouring under sore temptation; and this, Henry says, was in effect to give the cause on Satan's side, and to grant that Job had done the very thing the accuser had said he would do — cursed God to his face. To read a tempted saint's anguished words as blasphemy is to become the adversary's advocate.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, expounding the strophe, keep the emphasis on the outward sign that the inward turning betrays, the letting of "such words" go forth from the mouth; the spirit set against God vents itself in speech, and it is by Job's speech that Eliphaz presumes to read his heart. The witnesses do not divide over what Eliphaz alleges — a spirit turned against God and a mouth that overflows with the proof of it — but they divide sharply over its truth. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch trace the logic of the charge; Henry exposes its cruelty, that a friend should hear rebellion where God, who tried Job, heard only the groaning of a servant he would in the end vindicate. The reader, knowing the verdict of the last chapter, weighs Eliphaz's confident reading of the heart against the searcher of hearts who thought otherwise.
14:
"What is man, that he should be clean? and he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous?" With this the speech turns from Job's supposed crimes to the universal corruption of the race, and the witnesses recognise the note at once. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls it the ceaseless burden of the book, sounded already at ch. 4:17 and ch. 9:2 and to be sounded again at ch. 25:4; it is the great commonplace to which the friends perpetually return. Keil and Delitzsch render it as the flat impossibility that mortal man, or the man born flesh of a woman, should be entirely pure or sinless.

The reformed John Gill reads the question as put by way of contempt, to lessen man and abate any high conceit of himself. Man is not naturally clean, being conceived and born in sin; he cannot make himself clean by any means of his own; and however clean he may appear in his own eyes or in others', he is not clean in the sight of God — clean, indeed, only through the grace of God and the blood of Christ, which alone cleanses from all sin. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the force of the Hebrew word for "man," enosh, as weak, sickly, dying, miserable man, and reminds the reader that in the sacred writings natural birth was reckoned a defilement, every man coming into the world in a state of moral pollution; he suggests too that the verb might better be rendered "that he should justify himself" than "that he should be righteous."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses both the truth of the doctrine and the falseness of its application. Righteousness is a kind of cleanness, and man in his fallen state cannot pretend to it before God, being adjudged unclean because born of a woman, from whom he derives a corrupt nature that is at once his guilt and his pollution. So far Henry grants Eliphaz his point — indeed Job himself had said the very same at ch. 14:4, "who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" But does it follow, Henry asks, that Job is therefore the hypocrite and wicked man they charge him with being? By no means. Though man as born of a woman is not clean, yet as born again of the Spirit he is clean; and the general truth of human corruption, however sound, proves nothing against the particular integrity of one afflicted saint. The witnesses agree on the doctrine and part company on the inference Eliphaz would draw from it.
15:
To crush any pretension in man, Eliphaz reaches up to the heavens: "Behold, he putteth no trust in his saints; yea, the heavens are not clean in his sight." The reformed John Gill takes the "saints" first of holy men set apart by grace — an Abraham, an Isaac, a Jacob — whom God trusts with much, the prophets with his messages and the ministers with the treasure of the gospel, yet whom he trusts not with themselves, keeping their salvation and preservation in the hands of his Son and Spirit; though he grants that the Targum reads it of the saints above, the glorified and the angels. The point either way is that the purest creatures have no purity to stand upon of their own.

The grammatical-historical witnesses take the "holy ones" of the angels. Keil and Delitzsch identify them with the angels as beings of light, as at ch. 4:18, and refuse to flatten "the heavens" into a mere synonym for them. John Wesley, of the wesleyan-arminian school, agrees that the saints are the angels, God's holy ones of Deut. 33:2 and Ps. 103:20, many of whom, though created holy, fell; and he distinguishes carefully that the angels are pure from corruption but not from imperfection, none being pure simply and perfectly and in comparison with God. Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, gathers the older versions — the Vulgate, "among his saints none is immutable," and Coverdale, "he hath found unfaithfulness among his own saints" — and lays down the principle: nothing is immutable but God; saints may fall, angels may fall, all their goodness being derived and dependent, and the very heavens have no purity compared with his.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry crowns the thought with a memorable image borrowed from Caryl. God places no confidence in saints and angels, Henry says, but employs them while giving them fresh supplies of strength and wisdom, as knowing they are neither more nor better than his grace makes them; and he takes no complacency even in the heavens, which, pure as they seem to us, have in his eye many a speck and many a flaw. "If the stars have no light in the sight of the sun," Henry quotes, "what light has the sun in the sight of God?" — and he points to the day of Isa. 24:23, when the moon shall be confounded and the sun ashamed. The witnesses stand as one: if the brightest creatures are dim before God, no man may plead his own cleanness.
16:
From the impurity of the heavens Eliphaz draws his crushing conclusion about man: "How much more abominable and filthy is man, which drinketh iniquity like water!" The reformed John Gill reads it as the descent from the greater to the less: if the saints are not to be trusted and the heavens are not pure, much less this creature who in his natural, corrupt, unregenerate state is cast out to loathing, dead in trespasses and sins, abominable even to himself when once he is made sensible of it and comes to abhor himself and repent. He drinks iniquity, Gill says, because sin is of a defiling nature and man is naturally and originally filthy, conceived in sin, so that no clean thing can be brought out of the unclean.

Here a real difference of rendering divides the witnesses. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke argues that the Hebrew aph ki should be translated not "how much more" but "how much less": how much less, that is, would God confide in a man who is filthy and abominable and drinks down iniquity like water. On the figure itself all agree, and Clarke draws it out finely — a man under sinful propensities commits sin as greedily as a thirsty man or a thirsty camel drinks water, and thinks he can never have enough; it is the finished portrait of a bad man, who hungers and thirsts after sin as the good man hungers and thirsts after righteousness. John Wesley adds that such a man, beyond his native proneness, has contracted settled habits of sinning, and sins as freely and delightfully as men in those hot countries drink water.

The grammatical-historical voices weigh the intent. Charles Ellicott observes that language so strong, though couched in general terms, is doubtless meant to reflect on Job in particular, for otherwise it need not have been pitched so high; Keil and Delitzsch keep the sweep of it, "how much less the abominable and corrupt, man who drinketh iniquity as water." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the comparison home: if the saints are not to be trusted, much less sinners; if the heavens are not pure, much less man who is degenerated; and he drinks iniquity as greedily and with as much pleasure as a thirsty man drinks, as water to a man in a dropsy, so that the more men sin the more they would sin. So the witnesses stand together on the loathsomeness of sin and its thirsty appetite, dividing only over whether the particle mounts from man's impurity to God's mistrust as "how much more" or descends to it as "how much less."
17:
With his indictment of man complete, Eliphaz clears his throat for a fresh discourse: "I will shew thee, hear me; and that which I have seen I will declare." The reformed John Gill explains that Eliphaz now proceeds to illustrate and defend the proposition on which his whole censure rests — that only the wicked, and not the righteous, are afflicted of God, and afflicted especially in the terrible manner Job has been. He promises to set before Job things worthy of his regard, and not the vain and unprofitable stuff which, in his estimate, Job has been uttering; the offer to "shew" carries a note of condescension, as of a teacher stooping to instruct a wayward pupil.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds both the logic and the pride of the preface. Eliphaz, having reproved Job's answers, now comes to maintain the thesis on which he had built his censure: that the wicked are certainly miserable, whence he would infer, by a false conversion, that those who are miserable are certainly wicked, and that therefore Job is so. His solemn preface bespeaks Job's attention — "I will show thee that which is worth hearing, and not reason, as thou dost, with unprofitable talk" — and here Henry catches a familiar fault: men are apt, when they condemn the reasonings of others, to commend their own. Eliphaz promises to teach from two founts, and the first is his own experience: "that which I have myself seen, in divers instances, I will declare." It is of good use, Henry grants, to take notice of the providences of God among the children of men, and what good observations we have made and found benefit by, we should be ready to communicate for the benefit of others, and may speak boldly when we declare what we have seen.

Yet the witnesses leave a shadow over the confidence of the preamble. The very solemnity with which Eliphaz announces his lesson — the appeal to sight, to experience, to what he himself has witnessed — is the ground of its error, for he has seen much of the world's ordinary course and mistaken it for a law without exception. What he is about to declare, that calamity dogs the wicked and the wicked only, is true as far as it reaches and false where he applies it; and the reader who knows why Job suffers can hear, under the grave "I will shew thee," the tragedy of a man certain he is teaching wisdom while he is in fact building the case that God will overturn. Gill and Henry agree that the preface is offered in all sincerity, and that its sincerity is precisely what makes its misdirection so poignant.
18:
To his own observation Eliphaz joins the authority of tradition: "which wise men have told from their fathers, and have not hid it." The reformed John Gill weighs the word "wise" in its best sense, of men wise not to do evil but to do good, wise unto salvation, who would neither tell an untruth nor report a false or foolish thing but upon good testimony; and what such men had received from their fathers, themselves also wise and good, deserved regard even though it came by tradition and not by the witness of one's own eyes. The chain of trustworthy elders lends its weight to the doctrine he is about to press.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears Eliphaz here adopting the very language of Bildad at ch. 8:8, appealing at once to his own experience and to the universal tradition of an earlier age, before civil commotion and foreign disturbance had troubled the land. John Wesley, of the wesleyan-arminian school, marks the added clause "and have not hid it": the fathers judged the truth so certain and so important that they would not conceal it in their own breasts, but handed it on. Keil and Delitzsch begin here to unfold the doctrine itself, the long poetic portrait of the wicked man that runs through the strophe — the ungodly man who is sensible of pain all his days, the tyrant for whom a fixed tale of years is reserved, terrors sounding in his ears, the destroyer coming upon him in his peace.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the wholesome lesson out of the appeal to antiquity even while the argument built on it is going astray. The wisdom and learning of the moderns, he observes, are very much derived from those of the ancients; good children learn a great deal from their good parents, and what we have learned from our ancestors we must transmit to our posterity and not hide from the generations to come, as the psalmist charges in Ps. 78:3-6. If the thread of the knowledge of many ages be cut off by the carelessness of one, all that succeed fare the worse. So the witnesses honour the principle of received wisdom that Eliphaz invokes, while the reader remembers that a doctrine may be old and widely handed down and still be misapplied; the fathers' truth that calamity follows wickedness becomes a lie in the mouth that turns it against a righteous sufferer.
19:
Eliphaz commends his authorities as men of the first rank: "unto whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed among them." The reformed John Gill takes these not for mean or obscure men but for such as were entrusted with the government of whole kingdoms, appointed by God and honoured by men. He will not confine the phrase to the land of Canaan and the patriarchs, who probably had not yet enjoyed it; it looks rather, he thinks, to larger tracts of the earth and to earlier times, and very likely to Noah and his sons, to whom the whole earth was given after the flood, replenished by them and divided among them.

Here the witnesses genuinely divide over the reference. The wesleyan-arminian voices lean the other way. Adam Clarke judges that Eliphaz very likely means the Israelites, who received possession of the promised land from God himself, no stranger being suffered to dwell in it while its old inhabitants were driven out; he mentions the alternative of Noah and his sons, when there was no stranger in being, but thinks the words apply more clearly to Israel. John Wesley agrees that these were no obscure men but the most worthy and famous of their ages, to whom the earth — that is, its dominion and possession — was given by the gracious gift of God; and he hears in "no stranger passed among them" a direct thrust at Job, for God so watched over those holy men that no enemy could invade or spoil them, as the Sabeans and Chaldeans had spoiled Job, and would have watched over Job too had he been such a man. Wesley reads the whole verse as framed to confute Job's complaint at ch. 9:24 that the earth is given into the hand of the wicked.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the surface sense, that the authorities Eliphaz vouches were men of rank and figure, unto whom alone the earth was given, and who might therefore be supposed favourites of heaven and best capable of making sound observations upon its providences. The witnesses agree that Eliphaz is buttressing his inherited doctrine with the prestige of undisturbed and prosperous men, and part only over whether the "wise men" of pure and quiet possession are Noah's line, as Gill leans, or Israel in the land, as Clarke and Wesley prefer; and Wesley alone hears in the boast of a land no stranger troubled a pointed rebuke of the man whom strangers had lately stripped of everything.
20:
Now the inherited doctrine is stated in full: "The wicked man travaileth with pain all his days, and the number of years is hidden to the oppressor." The reformed John Gill probes what the pain may be. It may be the labour of sinning itself, for the wicked man conceives mischief in his heart and travails with it and brings forth a lie that ends in death; or the toil of getting wealth, which pierces him through with many sorrows; or the gnawing gripe of a guilty conscience — though Gill is careful to add that this cannot be said of every wicked man in respect of outward pain, many of them living at ease. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes the Hebrew verb mithcholel and reads it "he torments himself," so that the wicked man is a very self-tormentor, the sole author of his own sufferings and his own ruin; a life of sin, Clarke insists, is a life of misery, and he that will sin must suffer.

John Wesley, another wesleyan-arminian voice, sums the wretchedness as a life of care and fear and grief, from the wrath of God, the torments of his own mind, and his outward calamities; and he notes that Eliphaz names the "oppressor" in particular because he supposed Job guilty of that very sin, and set this portrait against Job's assertion, at ch. 12:6, of the safety and prosperity of such men. The oppressor, Wesley adds, knows not how short his life may be and so lives in continual fear of losing it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott insists on the syntax and colours the whole picture. The clause about the years, he says, is not an independent statement as the Authorized Version makes it, but reads "even the number of years that are laid up for the oppressor"; and what follows is a highly-coloured, poetical description of the tyrant, true to the character of the speaker who had already professed his eerie vision in ch. 4:12. A sound of terror is for ever in the oppressor's ears, Ellicott paraphrases, lest the spoiler swoop upon him in his very prosperity; and from this inward darkness, so painfully at odds with his outward wealth, he sees no escape, but lives like Damocles under a sword for ever hanging over him. The witnesses agree that Eliphaz's wicked man is inwardly wretched even when outwardly secure, though they differ over the exact spring of his torment — the toil of sin, the fear of loss, or the self-inflicted anguish of a guilty soul.
21:
The portrait of inward terror deepens: "A dreadful sound is in his ears: in prosperity the destroyer shall come upon him." The reformed John Gill turns the phrase over, "a voice, a sound of fears," and asks whether the fears are imaginary or real. Sometimes, he says, the wicked fear where no cause is, fleeing when none pursues, a very Magor-missabib, a terror on every side, like Cain who fancied every man that met him would slay him — such is the effect of a guilty conscience. Sometimes the fears are real: the extraordinary sound that once sent the Syrian host fleeing from their tents in 2 Kings 7, or the ordinary alarms of war and the reports of one calamity after another — a description, Gill hints, not far from Job's own case, with its dreadful tidings brought by messenger upon messenger.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke ties the terror to the tyrant's own cruelty. If the man be an oppressor, he can have no rest, being full of suspicion that the cruelties he has visited on others shall one day be visited on himself; and so, even in the midst of his prosperity, he looks for the destroyer to rush upon him. The dread is the natural harvest of a violent life, which can never feel secure because it knows what it has done to make others insecure.

John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, presses the paradox to its sharpest: even when the wicked man feels no actual evil, he is tormented with perpetual fears, and the destroyer, when he does come, comes suddenly and unexpectedly, breaking in upon a false peace. The grammatical-historical reading behind the verse — that this is poetry painting the inner life of the ungodly rather than a record of events — gives the witnesses their common ground: the misery Eliphaz describes is chiefly a misery of the mind, a peace undermined from within by the memory of wrong and the expectation of vengeance. It is a shrewd and even a true observation of the disquiet that dogs a guilty conscience; its error lies not in the picture but in the assumption that so wretched a man must be the sort of man Job is. The reader, hearing Gill's echo of Job's own messengers of calamity, feels how nearly Eliphaz's general truth has been aimed, and how wide of Job's real case it falls. Gill's careful sorting of the fears — some of them the mere phantoms of a guilty mind that flees where none pursues, some the real alarms of war and disaster — leaves the door open that a man may hear dreadful sounds in his ears, as Job had heard them, messenger upon messenger, and yet be no oppressor and no hypocrite at all.
22:
The wicked man's despair is fixed upon him: "He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword." The reformed John Gill offers a cluster of senses. When such a man lies down at night he despairs of ever seeing the morning, through fear of some enemy or robber or murderer; or, taking darkness for calamity, he cannot persuade himself he will ever be delivered out of the trouble he is in — and here, Gill suggests, Eliphaz glances at Job, who had no hope of being restored to his former prosperity, whereas the good man, though he sit in darkness, believes he shall be brought again to the light. Gill notes too that among the heathen neighbours of Eliphaz, the Idumeans, many were without the hope of a resurrection, and so believed in no deliverance out of the darkness of the grave.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke narrows the sense and rejects one reading outright. If the man take but a few steps in the dark, Clarke says, he expects the dagger of the assassin — this, he thinks, is the only meaning of the place. Some would understand it of a man who has no hope of a resurrection, no escape from the tomb; but this Clarke doubts, for in the days of the writer of this book the doctrine of a future judgment was understood in every part of the East where the knowledge of the true God was diffused. So a quiet difference opens between them: Gill allows the graver, other-worldly overtone that Clarke sets aside as anachronistic.

John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, keeps to the plain psychology of guilt. When the wicked man falls into trouble he despairs of deliverance, and that "by reason of his guilty conscience"; and besides the calamity already upon him, he lives in constant expectation of a greater, "the sword" standing here, Wesley notes, for any grievous affliction that hangs over him. The witnesses agree that the verse paints a mind shut up in hopelessness, its darkness within answering to the danger without; they differ only over how far the darkness reaches — whether it is the fear of the assassin's blade and the loss of this life, as Clarke will have it, or reaches on, as Gill allows, to the darkness of the grave and the want of any hope beyond it. Either way, the witnesses see, Eliphaz has taken Job's own despair of ever being restored and turned it into a mark of the reprobate, when the same hopelessness might as truly be the honest grief of a good man who cannot yet see the light, and who has said as much of his own darkened prospects without thereby confessing himself wicked.
23:
The oppressor is brought low to beggary: "He wandereth abroad for bread, saying, Where is it? he knoweth that the day of darkness is ready at his hand." The reformed John Gill hesitates between two pictures. The wandering may be that of a plunderer and robber, roving abroad to increase his substance; or, more likely, that of a man reduced to poverty, wandering from place to place and from door to door to beg his bread — the very curse invoked upon the wicked man's posterity in Ps. 109:10, that his children should be continual vagabonds and beg. The proud oppressor, on this reading, ends as a homeless mendicant.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes on that reversal with feeling. The man is reduced to a state of utmost indigence; he who was once in affluence now asks for a morsel of bread and can scarcely, even by begging, procure enough to sustain life. And the closing clause Clarke reads by the Hebrew, "ready at his hand" being literally "in his hand," in his very possession: as he cannot get bread, he knows that death is already within his grasp, the dark day close upon him. John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, adds only that this knowledge of the coming darkness springs, like the man's other terrors, from his own guilty conscience, which forewarns him of the doom it feels it has deserved.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, however, will not let the picture pass unexamined, and here he shows the honest scruple of the critic. This, he says, is one of the points at which the description seems inconsistent, because overdrawn: the same man cannot easily be both the prosperous tyrant of the surrounding verses and a beggar wandering for bread — except, Ellicott allows, that foraging as well as plunder may be the object of a marauder's raids, so that the wandering "for bread" might still belong to the restless life of the raider rather than to destitution. The tension Ellicott marks is real, and the witnesses feel it: Gill's very hesitation between the robber and the beggar is the same difficulty seen from within. What none of them doubts is the drift of Eliphaz's argument, that the wicked man's outward glory is hollow and hurrying toward a dark and hungry end; the debate is only whether the verse paints him already fallen into want, or still ranging abroad with the gnawing knowledge that want and darkness wait for him.
24:
The dread that has haunted the wicked man now masses against him like an army: "Trouble and anguish shall make him afraid; they shall prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle." The reformed John Gill reads the fear two ways. It may be that his present troubles, being so dismal and distressing, frighten him with the dread that worse are still to come; or it may be the terror of what he fears hereafter — that indignation and wrath, tribulation and anguish, which shall come, as Rom. 2:9 declares, upon every soul of man that doeth evil. Either way the man is overmastered by a fear he cannot fight.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the closing image into a vivid picture of a captain overwhelmed. The wicked man lives in continual fear of death; brought down by adversity and stripped of the goods he had heaped up by oppression, his life becomes a mark for the meanest assassin. And "as a king ready to the battle" Clarke expounds by a grim irony: the man's acts of wickedness are as numerous as the troops a king commands, yet when he comes to meet his enemy in the field he is not only deserted but slain by his own forces. Clarke seals it with Juvenal's line, that few tyrants go down to the shades by a dry death or with a quiet end — violence is the usual exit of the violent.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers a different construction of the same figure. Rather than the wicked man being like a king armed for war, Ellicott reads, "they prevail against him like a king"; the terrors close in upon him with royal, irresistible force, and he himself is destined to be like a ball — the tossed plaything of calamity, flung about as the wound-up ball is hurled in Isa. 22:18. So the witnesses divide, mildly, over the grammar of the last clause: whether trouble assaults the man as a king marches out to battle, mighty and prepared, or whether trouble prevails over him as a king overwhelms a beaten foe, tossing him like a ball. On the substance they are agreed. Eliphaz means that the terrors of a guilty life gather at the last into an overpowering host, and that the man who spread trouble abroad is at length routed by trouble he cannot withstand. The figure of the beleaguered king caps the movement begun several verses before: the dreadful sound in the ears, the destroyer in prosperity, the darkness with no return, the wandering for bread, and now the final assault — each a step in the closing-in of the very fears the wicked man had thought his power could hold at bay.
25:
Eliphaz now names the sin that has earned all this dread: "For he stretcheth out his hand against God, and strengtheneth himself against the Almighty." The reformed John Gill reads the stretched-out hand as the gesture of an enemy, for the wicked man is not merely a sinner but enmity itself against God, and all his sins are so many acts of hostility against the divine nature and will and law. Some sins, Gill grants, are more daring than others, committed in a bold and audacious manner like those of Sodom, and such as strike directly at the being and providence of God, or reject the evangelic revelation, for which Heb. 10:29 threatens the sorer punishment.

The wesleyan-arminian voices set the sin in the tyrant's prosperity. Adam Clarke pictures the man who, while in power, thought himself supreme, did not acknowledge the God by whom kings reign, and used his power not to protect but to oppress those he ruled, and so strengthened himself against the Almighty. John Wesley marks that Eliphaz now gives the reason of all the fore-mentioned calamities — the man's great wickedness, his sinning against God with a high hand; and Wesley cannot help exclaiming at the madness of it, that this poor worm should dare to fight against the omnipotent God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the tense and to a nice question of whose armour is meant. Because the man has stretched out his hand against God and behaved himself proudly, he runs upon him with a haughty neck and "the thick bosses of his bucklers," fully protected, as he supposes, against the vengeance of the Most High. The English version, Ellicott notes, with less probability represents the armour as being God's; on the contrary, it is the wicked man's own prosperity that has thus blinded and hardened him, the fat security of Deut. 32:15 and the pride of Ps. 17:10. So the witnesses divide over the shield: whether the bosses of the buckler belong to God, arming himself against the rebel, or, as Ellicott urges, to the wicked man, who charges heaven behind the false defences of his own wealth. On the enormity itself they are of one mind — that the root of the whole doom is a creature lifting his hand against his Maker, the little arm of a mortal stretched out against the Almighty. And here the covert application to Job becomes sharpest, for Eliphaz has traced every terror of the preceding verses to this one cause, insinuating that a man so afflicted must have first defied the God who afflicts him; the reader who knows Job's cause knows the insinuation is false, and that the hand Job has stretched out is not the fist of the rebel but the open palm of a man pleading to be heard.
26:
The rebel's charge is drawn in full: "He runneth upon him, even on his neck, upon the thick bosses of his bucklers." The witnesses divide sharply over the plainest question the verse asks — who runs upon whom. The reformed John Gill takes the wicked man for the assailant, running upon God with fury as the he-goat in Daniel's vision ran upon the ram, or as a combatant who flings down his distant weapons and closes in to take his adversary by the throat and throw him to the ground; or else the phrase means that the man runs on "with his neck," with the stretched-out neck and iron sinew of insolence, his brow like brass. John Wesley, of the wesleyan-arminian school, reads it the same way: the wicked man comes close like a stout warrior to grapple with his foe, acting in flat opposition to God's precepts and providences, and pressing his attack even at the thick bosses of the buckler, where the enemy is strongest.

But Adam Clarke, another wesleyan-arminian voice, reverses the direction of the charge. Following Calmet, he refers the running to God himself, who like a mighty conquering hero marches against the ungodly, rushes upon him, and seizes him by the throat, which the mail encircling it cannot protect; neither shield nor spear can save the man when the Lord of hosts comes against him. On this reading it is not the rebel storming heaven but heaven storming the rebel, and the bosses of the buckler are the last vain defence that God's onset sweeps aside.

The grammatical-historical witnesses keep to the first construction. Keil and Delitzsch render it of the man who "assailed Him with a stiff neck, with the thick bosses of his shield," the very picture of proud defiance; and this coheres with Ellicott's reading of the preceding verse, that the bucklers are the wicked man's own. So the debate stands: is the verse the climax of the sinner's insolence, charging God neck outstretched behind his shield, as Gill, Wesley, and the grammatical-historical voices hold; or is it the beginning of God's terrible answer, the Almighty rushing upon the throat of the man whose armour cannot save him, as Clarke with Calmet would have it? The witnesses agree only that the image is one of headlong, close-quarters violence between the creature and his Maker — and that, whichever way the charge runs, it can end but one way.
27:
Eliphaz traces the rebel's insolence to his pampered ease: "Because he covereth his face with his fatness, and maketh collops of fat on his flanks." The reformed John Gill reads the fatness as the sign of overflowing prosperity: the man has no fear of God and no shame for his sin, because he abounds in riches and affluence, and this fulness makes him haughty and imperious. He is a very Jeshurun, who, as Deut. 32:15 records, waxed fat and grew thick and covered with fatness, and then kicked against God, forsaking the God that made him and lightly esteeming the Rock of his salvation. Prosperity, on Gill's reading, is the soil in which the man's defiance of heaven has grown rank.

The wesleyan-arminian voices sound the same note. John Wesley makes the fatness the express reason of the man's insolent carriage toward God: because he was fat, rich, potent, and successful — the very language of Ps. 78:31 and Jer. 46:21 — his great prosperity made him proud and secure and regardless of God and men, his only care to pamper himself. Adam Clarke pictures him as a man overloaded with flesh, who for very grossness cannot defend himself against the strong gripe of his adversary; and Clarke adds a curious flourish from the Arabic, which for "maketh collops of fat on his flanks" reads that he "lays the Pleiades upon the Hyades" — a proverb for boundless ambition, as of the giants who piled mountain upon mountain to scale heaven, until, as Virgil sang, the Father's thunderbolt laid their heaped-up works in ruins. To the lust of power there are no bounds, Clarke moralises, but the haughty spirit goes before a fall, and such a man's heaven is soon reduced to a chaos.

The witnesses do not divide over the sense; they agree that the verse names luxury and gross prosperity as the nurse of impiety, the well-fed security that forgets God. It is a shrewd observation, and a true one, that ease and abundance often breed contempt of heaven; and yet, set in Eliphaz's argument, it carries a covert thrust at Job, as though his former wealth had been of this fattening, God-forgetting kind. The reader who remembers Job's charity in his prosperity may weigh the insinuation and find it false, even while granting the general truth that a pampered flesh is a poor keeper of the fear of God. Wesley presses that truth to its moral edge: it was prosperity itself that made the man proud and secure and regardless of God and men, so that the very abundance meant to lead him to thankfulness became instead the occasion of his forgetting the giver — a warning that riches, though no sin in themselves, are a dangerous trust, and that the fat and easy heart must watch itself the more.
28:
The wicked man is next set among ruins: "And he dwelleth in desolate cities, and in houses which no man inhabiteth, which are ready to become heaps." Here the witnesses divide over whether the verse still paints his pride or has begun to paint his punishment. The reformed John Gill offers first the reading of prosperity: such is the man's might that he destroys the cities and palaces others had built, and then out of their ruins raises greater cities and nobler palaces to perpetuate his own name — a sense, he notes, that the Targum favours. On this construction the desolate cities are the monuments of his conquering ambition, not of his fall.

The other witnesses read it rather as the turn from glory to judgment. John Wesley says plainly that this verse is fitly opposed to the prosperity last mentioned, and is the beginning of the description of the man's misery. Adam Clarke pictures the tyrant reduced to inhabit the very cities his wars had ruined, dwelling in a house so decayed as to be ready to fall into heaps, a fate, he says, of which ancient and modern history afford abundant examples. And the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weight the clause toward a divine appointment: the desolated cities are not those the man himself has laid waste, for the phrase "which are ready to become heaps" points to a curse decreed upon them; they cite the law forbidding the rebuilding of cities laid under the ban in Deut. 13:16 and the example of 1 Kings 16:34, though they judge that no such precise play on the Mosaic law is intended, and take it more generally of a man who settles down carelessly and indolently, with no fear of the judgments of God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott completes the portrait of the haughty tyrant without quite deciding the tense: he dwelt in cities that are to be desolate, or that are already desolate, ready to become heaps — a phrase that may point to what the man intended them to be, or to what he had made them, or to what, in the speaker's judgment, they were likely to become, for all his fortifying and dwelling in them. So the debate is real. Is the man building splendour upon the ruins he has made, as Gill and the Targum allow, or is he already sinking into the ruins that judgment has decreed, as Wesley, Clarke, and Keil and Delitzsch take it? The witnesses agree only that the desolate city is somehow the wicked man's proper dwelling, whether as the trophy of his violence or the beginning of his doom.
29:
The doom itself is now pronounced upon the man's estate: "He shall not be rich, neither shall his substance continue, neither shall he prolong the perfection thereof upon the earth." The reformed John Gill dwells on the frustration of a life bent wholly on gain. Though the man's heart is set on riches and he labours for them with all his might, he shall not attain what he so covets; many take great pains to be rich, even in a lawful way, and are men of understanding in business, and yet riches are not their portion. Some gather much and never grow rich, putting their gain into a bag with holes; and such a man, whatever he heaps up, is poor in his own account, always craving more, and poor above all toward God.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the whole remainder of the chapter, and this verse first, as aimed directly at Job, whom Eliphaz would insinuate to have been a tyrant and oppressor. He counts off the threatened evils: the man shall not be rich, though he labour greatly for it; his substance shall not continue, for God will blast it; and he shall not prolong its perfection, for all his works shall perish and God will blot out his remembrance from under heaven. John Wesley states the middle clause with blunt brevity: what the man had gotten shall be taken from him.

The grammatical-historical witnesses labour over the obscure last word. Keil and Delitzsch note that this is where the conclusion of the strophe begins — he shall not be rich, his substance shall not stand — and that the closing term minlam is genuinely hard: it will not bear the older rendering "he shall not extend himself upon the earth," and the ancient guesses, whether "from them," or "their word," or the Septuagint's "shadow" and Jerome's "root," all fail to satisfy. Charles Ellicott agrees that the word rendered "perfection thereof" occurs nowhere else and is very doubtful, offering as alternatives "neither shall their produce bend luxuriantly to the earth," or their possessions and achievements extend upon it. The witnesses do not divide over the drift, which is plain enough — that the oppressor's wealth is fated to fail and leave nothing behind — but they confess honestly that the exact figure in the third clause is beyond sure recovery. What survives every doubt of the philology is Eliphaz's confident sentence, that riches gathered against God will neither grow, nor last, nor spread.
30:
The sentence darkens into images of fire and withering: "He shall not depart out of darkness; the flame shall dry up his branches, and by the breath of his mouth shall he go away." The reformed John Gill lets the darkness carry more than one weight. It is first the darkness of poverty and calamity, out of which the man despairs of ever coming; but Gill hears also, beneath the temporal ruin, the darkness of sin and unregeneracy that he does not forsake, and beyond that again the outer blackness of darkness reserved for him, out of which, once entered, there is no departing at all. The wicked man's night, on this reading, deepens from misfortune to guilt to final doom.

The wesleyan-arminian voices take the burning and the blast as figures of judgment. Adam Clarke reads the drying of the branches as the cutting off of the man's children by sudden judgments, and "by the breath of his mouth shall he go away" as the ease with which God slays the wicked — for by the breath of his mouth God destroys them. John Wesley expounds the several figures in turn: his misery shall have no end; the flame is the anger and judgment of God; his branches are the wealth and power and glory that encompassed him as branches a tree; and "by the breath of his mouth" shows with how little effort God subdues his enemies, one word, one blast, one act of his will sufficing. Wesley notes too that the Hebrew is "go back," so that the man runs away from God faster than he had run upon him at v.26 — the conflict of the earlier verses continued to its rout.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott points back to the darkness first named at v.22 and confesses that the last clause is not very clear, offering that "by the breath of his mouth shall he go away" may mean, as in ch. 11:20, that when he expires it shall be the end of him, leaving nothing permanent behind; or that he shall pass away suddenly and completely, like his own breath. So a small difference runs beneath the agreement, over whose branches and whose breath are meant — whether the flame consumes the man's children, as Clarke has it, or his encircling glory, as Wesley reads, and whether the fatal breath is God's destroying blast or the man's own last expiring sigh. The witnesses agree that the verse seals the oppressor's ruin as total and swift, a darkness he cannot leave and a fire that spares neither him nor his.
31:
Eliphaz breaks off his portrait to warn against the delusion that fed it: "Let not him that is deceived trust in vanity: for vanity shall be his recompence." The reformed John Gill anatomises the deception. Every wicked man is deceived — by Satan, who deceives the whole world and deceived our first parents; or by his own deceitful and desperately wicked heart; or through the deceitfulness of sin, which promises profit and pleasure and liberty and pays in ruin and bondage, and through the deceitfulness of riches, which promise a satisfaction they never give. Such a man is prone to trust in vanity, in men who are altogether vanity, in creature enjoyments that are vexation of spirit, in his own heart, and in his righteousness and privileges; and from all such empty confidence the verse dehorts him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the warning as the seventh of the evils he has been numbering against the wicked man: he has many vain imaginations of obtaining wealth and power and pleasure and happiness, but he is deceived, for he has trusted in a lie, and this lie is the very recompence he shall receive. John Wesley widens the caution beyond the single figure to a general lesson for all men, that they take heed of running into the same error and mischief; and he plays finely on the word "recompence," which the Hebrew makes "his exchange" — the man shall exchange one vanity for another, bartering a pleasing vanity for a vexatious one, his imagined felicity for disappointment and dissatisfaction and loss.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would render the clause "let him not trust in vanity, deceiving himself," turning the deception inward upon the man's own self-flattery, and he sets it beside the self-deceiving religion of James 1:26 and the empty things that cannot profit nor deliver in 1 Sam. 12:21. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the verse gathers the whole preceding portrait into a single moral, that the wicked man's prosperity is a vanity in which it is madness to trust, and that the trust and the vanity are of a piece, so that the empty thing a man leans on becomes the empty reward he is paid with. Whether the deceit is charged to Satan, to sin, or to the man himself, the lesson is one: to build on vanity is to be recompensed with vanity. The caution reaches, on Wesley's reading, past the single wicked man to every hearer, a warning that the felicity of the ungodly is a thing no one should envy or lean upon, since it is already sentenced to dissolve into the very disappointment it conceals; and there is a quiet irony that Eliphaz should preach against trusting in vanity to a man who has just been stripped of every earthly thing, and who is learning, in the ash-heap, to trust in nothing but God.
32:
The wicked man's ruin is timed to fall untimely: "It shall be accomplished before his time, and his branch shall not be green." The reformed John Gill takes the "it" first of the recompence just named, the punishment of a life of vanity, which shall come upon the man "before his day," before old age, before the natural evening of his years. Or he reads the clause of the man's life itself, filled up and cut short before its time — not before the time fixed in the purpose of God, but before the term that he and his friends had reckoned on, before the common span of human life; and so the verse foretells an immature and premature death, the branch withered before it could ripen.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke leans on the Vulgate, "he shall perish before his time, before his days are completed," and reads the double doom accordingly: the man shall be removed by a violent death and not live out half his days, and "his branch shall not be green," for there shall be no scion from his root and all his posterity shall fail. John Wesley agrees that the accomplishing is of the vanity that shall be his recompence, and that "before his time" means when, by the course of nature and common providence, he might have continued much longer.

The grammatical-historical witnesses look to the whole close of the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch, opening the last strophe, render the coming lines of the withering branch and the vine that casts its unripe grapes and the olive that sheds its flower, and read the "day not yet" as the doom that ripens before its season. Charles Ellicott takes "it shall be accomplished" as "paid in full before its time," and observes that the remainder of the chapter calls for little explanation, being only the orthodox and familiar saw that the wicked are punished in this life, and by implication the good rewarded — a maxim, Ellicott adds pointedly, that fails utterly in the face of afflictions like Job's, unless, as the friends insinuate, Job be reckoned among the wicked.
