The witnesses agree that the verse decrees a premature and childless end; and Ellicott alone lifts his eyes from the doctrine to the sufferer, and marks how the whole confident scheme shatters against the innocent man on the ash-heap. For the maxim is not false in itself — the wicked do often come to untimely and barren ruin — but it is fatal as an instrument of diagnosis, since it reasons backward from the affliction to the guilt, and so must number every sufferer among the sinners. It is the very engine of the friends' error, and Job's whole case is the standing refutation of it.
33:
The image of the withered branch is drawn out into the vineyard and the olive-yard: "He shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and shall cast off his flower as the olive." The reformed John Gill turns the figure several ways. It may be the wicked man himself who shakes off and loses his substance; or God who shakes from him all that was dear and valuable; or the man who is shaken by one providence after another, as a vine is shaken by a violent wind and tempest, its unripe grapes battered off by a hailstorm, or plucked away, or dropping through rottenness. So, Gill says, is the wicked man suddenly stripped of his wealth, or his children snatched from him in their youth, before they are grown to maturity, and thus like the unripe grape; and he suspects that Eliphaz has an eye here to Job's own case, both in his ruined substance and in his lost family.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the two figures wholly of the man's posterity. Whatever children he may have shall never survive him nor come to mature age, but shall be like wind-fall grapes and blasted olive blossoms, dropping before their season. And Clarke lingers on the fitness of the two trees chosen: the vine and the olive are among the most useful of all trees, yielding the wine and the oil so necessary for the worship of God and the comfort of man; and so they may aptly stand for the hopeful progeny of the oppressor, who fell, like the untimely grape and the blasted olive-flower, without ever living to fulfil the public expectation that had rested on them.

The two witnesses stand together over the sorrow the image carries, and it is worth marking how much of the chapter's cruelty gathers into this single verse. For if Gill is right that Eliphaz glances at Job, then the picture of a vine casting its unripe grapes and an olive shedding its flower is aimed at the freshest of Job's wounds, the ten children swept away in a day; and the doctrine that a wicked man's offspring perish untimely is pressed, however unwittingly, upon a father whose offspring have indeed perished. The witnesses do not divide over the sense of the metaphor — a life stripped of its fruit before the fruit could ripen — but the reader, hearing it, feels the full weight of what it is to comfort a bereaved man by telling him that childlessness is the mark of the wicked. What Eliphaz means for a general warning falls, in Job's ears, as a particular and undeserved reproach.
34:
The doom widens from the man to his whole circle: "For the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate, and fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery." The reformed John Gill fixes on the word "hypocrites" — men who seem what they are not, outwardly righteous before men but inwardly wicked, having a form of godliness but denying its power, as 2 Tim. 3:5 describes. Eliphaz speaks not of one hypocrite but of a congregation, a society, even a family of them, and Gill suspects a covert glance at Job's own household, now reduced to desolation and want; or the word may mean "solitary," destitute of friends and of the comforts of life, and may reach on to the future state of such men, bidden at last to depart, with no society among the angels and the saints.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch press the Hebrew of "desolate," the word galmud, which they render a hard, lifeless, stony mass, stark and dead; the family-circle of the ungodly, they say, is left barren and lifeless, while fire devours the tents of bribery, the dwellings raised or maintained by corrupt gain. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in it two fresh insinuations against Job. To speak of the "congregation" or society of hypocrites as coming to a barren rock — the same word, he notes, that is used at ch. 3:7 — is to class Job among the impious; and to say that "fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery" is to hint that Job had perverted justice and taken bribes.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the same pointed echo. "Desolate" was Job's own word, used by him at ch. 3:7, and being an uncommon word there may well be an intentional reference to his use of it, Eliphaz turning Job's lament for the night of his birth into a sentence upon Job's whole house. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the verse is the sharpest of Eliphaz's covert thrusts, gathering hypocrisy, corruption, and desolation into one indictment and aiming it, under cover of a general maxim, at the very man he came to comfort; and the reader who knows Job's integrity hears the injustice of it, that a righteous sufferer should be numbered with the takers of bribes and the congregation of the false. Gill's suggestion that the desolate "congregation" glances at Job's ruined household gives the thrust its cruelty, for Job's family had indeed been swept away; and Ellicott's ear for the echo of Job's own word makes it crueler still, as though Eliphaz had taken up the very language in which Job cursed the day of his birth and turned it into a verdict upon Job's whole house — the accuser borrowing the sufferer's grief to prove the sufferer's guilt.
35:
Eliphaz ends his speech with a proverb of monstrous birth: "They conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity, and their belly prepareth deceit." The reformed John Gill reads it plainly of the wicked persons he has been describing: they meditate sin in their minds, and contrive how to commit it, and form within themselves schemes to do mischief to others. The figure is of a settled and inward wickedness, hatched deliberately and delivered as its own kind.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the elegance of the image and its terrible logic. The wicked conceive mischief from the seed which Satan sows in their hearts; in producing it they travail with many pangs, for sin is a sore labour; and at last their womb brings forth fraud and deception — an accursed birth from an iniquitous conception. Clarke sets it beside the fuller statement of the same figure by James, that when lust hath conceived it bringeth forth sin, and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death, in James 1:15. And then, the long indictment ended, Clarke turns with sudden tenderness to the man on the ash-heap: poor Job, he cries, what a siege of affliction had he to sustain — his body wasted with disease, his mind harassed by Satan, and his heart wrung by the unkindness and false accusations of his friends; no wonder he was greatly agitated, often distracted, and sometimes even thrown off his guard. Yet all his enemies were chained, and beyond that chain they could not go, for God was his unseen Protector and did not suffer his faithful servant to be greatly moved.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the vividness of the figure, comparing the like conceiving and travailing of iniquity in Ps. 7:14 and Isa. 59:4: the wicked hatch the sorrow and mischief of others, and what their inward part prepares recoils in evil upon themselves. So the speech closes as it began, with the settled conviction that wickedness is self-punishing, that the deceit conceived in the heart is a birth that devours its parent. The witnesses agree on the sense of the proverb, and Clarke alone lifts the reader's eye from the general doctrine to the particular sufferer, reminding us that this whole grim anatomy of the wicked has been recited over a righteous man, and that the God whom Eliphaz invokes against Job is the very God who stands, unseen, as Job's protector and will not let him be finally moved.
